ox: Incorrect. Positron emission is for nuclides with too FEW neutrons (below the band). It turns a proton into a neutron.
Incorrect. Electron capture also fixes too FEW neutrons (proton-rich nuclides) by turning a proton into a neutron.
Correct. Too many neutrons for the protons means above the band of stability. β⁻ decay turns a neutron into a proton (n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino), lowering the neutron-to-proton ratio.
Incorrect. Gamma emission releases energy from an excited nucleus but does not change the numbers of protons or neutrons, so it cannot fix a neutron excess.

concept.t: Decay modes and the band of stability
p: Stable nuclei sit along a 'band of stability'. Nuclides above the band have too many neutrons and fix this by β⁻ decay (neutron → proton). Nuclides below the band have too few neutrons and use β⁺ decay or electron capture (proton → neutron). Very heavy nuclei (Z > 83) often emit alpha particles.

x4E_014.trap: Choosing positron emission because it sounds like it 'adds' protons. Positron emission REMOVES a proton.
x4E_014.eli: A team with too many players on one side shifts one player to the other side. The nucleus turns a neutron into a proton.
mem: Too many neutrons (above the band) → β⁻: n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino.
Too few neutrons (below the band) → β⁺ or electron capture: p → n.
Heavy nuclei (Z > 83) → alpha decay.
x4E_014.sc: Too many N → turn an N into a P → β⁻ (the electron leaves, the nucleus gains a proton).
x4E_014.mn: Neutron-rich → Negative beta. Proton-rich → Positive beta (or EC).

ox: Incorrect. The heavy daughter nucleus carries away very little of the energy because it is so much heavier than the electron. Recoil alone cannot explain a full continuous range of electron energies; the missing particle is the antineutrino.
Incorrect. Electrons do not lose varying energy in the electron cloud; they leave the atom essentially unimpeded and are detected with a continuous spread.
Incorrect. Identical nuclei of one nuclide release the SAME total decay energy every time. If it varied from nucleus to nucleus, the spread would not match the observed shape.

Correct. In β⁻ decay (n → p + e⁻ + ν̄) the total energy is fixed, but it is shared randomly between the electron and the antineutrino. The electron can therefore carry anything from nearly 0 up to the full amount, giving a continuous spectrum.

p: Alpha particles and gamma photons come in fixed energies because those decays have only two bodies sharing the energy. Beta decay has THREE bodies (daughter nucleus, electron and antineutrino), so the energy split can vary. The antineutrino was first proposed to rescue energy conservation in this exact observation.

x4E_028.trap: Blaming the nucleus for different energies; identical nuclei release the same total energy.
x4E_028.eli: Two kids share a fixed bag of 10 candies; one can get any number from 0 to 10, as long as the two shares add to 10.
mem: β⁻: n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino (ν̄).
Energy is shared randomly between e⁻ and ν̄, so the electron energy is continuous.
Alpha and gamma have discrete energies; beta has a spread up to a maximum.
x4E_028.sc: Single fixed energies = two-body decay. A spread of energies = three-body decay.
x4E_028.mn: Alpha and gamma are Always-the-same; beta is Broad.

ox: Incorrect. 500 nm would mean the second photon has the same energy as the absorbed one. That would send out twice as much energy as came in.
Correct. Energy ∝ 1/λ. In units of 1/1000 nm: absorbed 500 nm = 2, first emitted 1000 nm = 1. Two in, one out, so the other must be 1 → λ = 1000 nm.
Incorrect. 1500 nm adds the wavelengths (500 + 1000). Wavelengths do not add; ENERGIES do, and energy goes as 1/λ.
Incorrect. 333 nm comes from adding the energies of the 500 and 1000 nm photons (2 + 1 = 3) instead of subtracting the emitted one from the absorbed one.

p: A photon's energy is E = hc/λ, so energy is proportional to 1/λ. When an atom absorbs a photon and relaxes in two steps, the total energy emitted equals the energy absorbed. So: 1/λ(absorbed) = 1/λ₁ + 1/λ₂.

x4E_064.eli: Think of 1/λ as 'energy coins'. A 500 nm photon is worth 2 coins and a 1000 nm photon is worth 1 coin. Two coins in, one coin out, so the other must be worth 1 coin.
mem: E = hc/λ: shorter wavelength = more energy.
Energy is conserved: energy in = sum of energies out.
Add ENERGIES (1/λ), never wavelengths.

fm.f: E = h·c / λ, so E ∝ 1/λ, where E = photon energy, h = Planck's constant, c = speed of light, λ = wavelength
fm.v: Use units of 1/1000 nm: absorbed (500 nm) = 2; first emitted (1000 nm) = 1; second emitted = x
fm.why: We use 1/λ because photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, and energy is what is conserved.

x4E_064.sc: Count coins in 1/1000 units: 500 nm = 2, 1000 nm = 1.
x4E_064.mn: Short = Strong: a shorter wavelength carries more energy.

ox: Correct. Level gaps shrink as n rises, so the 2-to-1 gap is bigger than the 3-to-2 gap. A bigger gap gives a photon with more energy and a shorter wavelength.
Wrong. Less energy would indeed pair with longer wavelength, but the 2-to-1 gap is the larger one.
Wrong. This pairs high energy with long wavelength, which cannot happen because E = hc/wavelength. Energy and wavelength move in opposite directions.
Wrong. Different transitions have different gaps and give photons of different energy. Assuming equal energy is the trap.

p: An electron in an atom sits in levels numbered n = 1, 2, 3 and so on. When it drops to a lower level, it releases a photon whose energy equals the gap between the levels.
The levels are close together at high n and far apart near n = 1. So jumps to or from n = 1 are the biggest.

d_4E_12.eli: Like stairs that get taller near the ground floor. Dropping the last step to the ground is the biggest drop.
mem: Photon energy = energy gap between levels
Gaps shrink as n increases
Bigger energy means shorter wavelength
d_4E_12.trap: Assuming every drop to a lower level releases the same energy.

ox: Correct. Ionization energy (energy to remove an electron) rises across a period. Neon, a noble gas with a full shell, holds its electrons most tightly of these choices.
Wrong. Sodium has one loosely held outer electron, so its ionization energy is very low.
Wrong. Magnesium is a metal, with a low ionization energy compared with the nonmetals.

Wrong. Fluorine is high, but neon sits one step further right in the same period with a filled shell and a higher value. The trap is confusing electronegativity (fluorine highest) with ionization energy.

p: First ionization energy is the energy needed to pull off the outermost electron from an atom. It is high when the electron is held tightly.
Across a period (left to right) the nucleus gains protons, so the pull grows. Up a group, atoms are smaller, so it also grows. Helium and neon are the top.

d_4E_14.eli: Like pulling a toy from a child's hand. A child gripping it tightly (neon) is hardest to beat.
mem: Ionization energy increases left to right and bottom to top
Noble gases are highest in their period
Metals lose electrons easily
d_4E_14.trap: Picking fluorine because it has the highest electronegativity. Noble gases are excluded from electronegativity but top ionization energy.

ox: Wrong. Neon has a full shell, so it does not want another electron. Its electron affinity is near zero or unfavorable.
Wrong. Sodium gains an electron only weakly. It prefers to lose one.
Wrong. Magnesium has a filled 3s subshell, so adding an electron is near zero or unfavorable.

Correct. Chlorine is one electron short of a full octet and strongly attracts one. Its electron affinity is the most exothermic of these (and even more than fluorine, whose tiny size causes crowding).

p: Electron affinity is the energy change when an atom gains an electron. If energy is released (exothermic), the atom likes the extra electron.
Halogens are one electron from a full outer shell, so they have the strongest affinities. Noble gases and filled subshells do not want another electron.

d_4E_16.eli: Like a puzzle missing one piece. The piece snaps in happily. A finished puzzle (neon) has no space.
mem: Halogens have the most exothermic electron affinity
Chlorine slightly beats fluorine
Noble gases and Group 2 are near zero
d_4E_16.trap: Assuming fluorine must be highest in everything. Its small size makes electron crowding.

ox: Correct. Hund's rule says electrons fill separate orbitals of equal energy first, all with the same (parallel) spin. Nitrogen's three 2p electrons sit in three different p orbitals, spins parallel.
Wrong. Pairing two electrons in one p orbital while another stays empty breaks Hund's rule. The trap is pairing too early.
Wrong. Separate orbitals is right, but spins should be parallel. Antiparallel spins lose the stability Hund's rule gives.
Wrong. Three electrons cannot be fully paired in two orbitals; one would be unpaired. Pairs need two electrons each.

p: The three 2p orbitals have the same energy. Hund's rule says electrons spread out one per orbital, all spinning the same way, before any pair up.
This lowers repulsion between electrons. Nitrogen therefore has three unpaired electrons, making it paramagnetic.

d_4E_20.eli: Like kids on a bus choosing seats. Each takes an empty row first before anyone sits beside another.
mem: Fill degenerate orbitals singly first, parallel spins
Pair up only after every orbital has one electron
Unpaired electrons mean paramagnetic
d_4E_20.trap: Pairing electrons before every orbital in the subshell has one.

ox: Wrong. Intensity does not change each photon's energy. KEmax depends on frequency, which is fixed.
Correct. KEmax = hf - phi depends only on frequency. More intensity means more photons, so more electrons are ejected, each with the same maximum kinetic energy.
Wrong. More photons hit the metal, so more electrons come out, not fewer.
Wrong. The threshold frequency depends on the metal's work function, a property of the material, not the light intensity.

p: When light hits a metal, a photon can knock out an electron if the photon has enough energy. The minimum energy needed is the work function (phi). Below the threshold frequency, no electrons leave.
Each photon hits one electron. Photon energy depends on frequency. Intensity only sets how many photons arrive.

d_4E_26.eli: Throwing tennis balls at a window. Faster balls (higher frequency) break it with more force. Throwing more balls does not make any single ball faster.
mem: KEmax = hf - phi
Frequency sets KEmax; intensity sets number of electrons
Threshold frequency is set by the metal

fm.f: KEmax = hf - phi, where KEmax = top kinetic energy of ejected electrons, h = Planck's constant, f = light frequency, phi = work function
fm.v: f is fixed, phi is fixed
fm.s: KEmax stays the same since neither f nor phi changed
fm.why: Each electron absorbs one photon, so only photon energy matters.
fm.nc: No numbers needed; just see what changed.

d_4E_26.trap: Using the classical wave idea that brighter light means more energetic electrons.

ox: Wrong. Full s subshells alone would not give color or variable oxidation states. The key feature is the partly filled d orbitals.
Wrong. Transition metals have low to moderate electronegativity, and electronegativity does not cause color.
Wrong. They do have valence electrons, in the ns and (n-1)d orbitals.

Correct. Partly filled d orbitals have closely spaced energy levels, so electrons can jump between them by absorbing visible light (color). Also ns and (n-1)d energies are similar, so different numbers of electrons can be lost.

p: Transition metals have partly filled d orbitals. In compounds these d orbitals split into slightly different energies.
Electrons absorb visible light to jump between them. This is a d-d transition, and the leftover light is the color we see. Since ns and d electrons are close in energy, several oxidation states form.

d_4E_30.eli: Like a ladder with rungs very close together. Small amounts of light are enough to hop between rungs.
mem: Partially filled d orbitals give color (d-d transitions)
ns and (n-1)d energies are similar, so multiple oxidation states
Many are paramagnetic
d_4E_30.trap: Blaming electronegativity. Color comes from d-orbital energy gaps.

ox: Wrong. Electrons added across a period enter the same shell and shield each other poorly, so Zeff does not drop.
Correct. Going from Na to Cl, protons increase from 11 to 17 while inner-shell shielding stays about the same, so the pull on valence electrons (Zeff) rises and the atom shrinks.
Wrong. Zeff does not stay constant because the number of protons keeps increasing.
Wrong. Shells are not added across a period. New shells appear when moving down a group.

p: Zeff is the pull a valence electron actually feels from the nucleus after inner electrons block some of it. This blocking is called shielding.
Across a period, each step adds a proton. Electrons added go into the same shell and barely shield each other. So the pull increases and atoms get smaller.

d_4E_37.eli: A magnet gets stronger while the same paper sheet sits in between. The pull on a paperclip grows.
mem: Zeff increases left to right across a period
Same-shell electrons shield poorly
Radius shrinks across a period
d_4E_37.trap: Thinking more electrons always means more shielding. Same-shell electrons barely shield.

ox: Wrong. Two valence electrons would show the big jump after the second value (between 1817 and 2745). The jump here is later.
Wrong. Four valence electrons would put the huge jump after the fourth value. There is no fifth value showing that.
Correct. The values rise gradually (577, 1817, 2745) then leap to 11,577. The fourth electron comes from an inner shell, so there are three valence electrons (Group 13, like aluminum).
Wrong. One valence electron would put the huge jump after the first value. The jump position, not the first value, tells the count.

p: Each time you remove an electron, the next one is harder to remove. Removing valence electrons is moderately hard.
When you start removing an inner-shell electron, the energy jumps hugely because inner electrons are close to the nucleus. The jump tells you how many valence electrons there are.

d_4E_40.eli: Peeling an onion. The outer layers come off easily, but the layer just below is stuck on much harder.

Valence electrons = number of electrons removed before the jump
Group 13 has a jump after IE3

ox: Wrong. Neutron-to-proton conversion is beta decay and does not explain why a stable nucleus weighs less than its parts.
Wrong. Nucleons are conserved; none vanish.
Correct. When nucleons bind together, energy is released (the binding energy). By E = mc^2 this energy corresponds to lost mass, so the nucleus weighs less than the separate nucleons.
Wrong. Electron shielding is an atomic effect, not a nuclear one, and does not change nuclear mass.

p: The mass defect is the small difference between the mass of the separate protons and neutrons and the mass of the nucleus they form. The nucleus is lighter.

The missing mass was released as energy when the nucleus formed. E = mc^2 links the two, where c is the speed of light. That energy is the binding energy, which would be needed to pull the nucleus apart.

d_4E_9.eli: Like a magnet set that gives off a click of energy when it snaps together. To break it apart, you must put that energy back.

Mass defect x c^2 = binding energy
Greater binding energy per nucleon means more stable

ox: Correct. An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons). Losing it lowers mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2.
Wrong. Losing protons lowers atomic number, so it cannot go up by 2. The trap is a sign error.
Wrong. Mass unchanged with atomic number +1 describes beta-minus decay, where a neutron becomes a proton.
Wrong. Mass unchanged with atomic number -1 describes beta-plus decay or electron capture.

p: Alpha decay is when a heavy nucleus ejects an alpha particle, which is a helium-4 nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Mass number (protons plus neutrons) drops by 4. Atomic number (protons) drops by 2.
The new element is two places to the left on the periodic table.

ox: Correct. Each half-life cuts the amount in half: 1/2, then 1/4, then 1/8. 1/8 = 12.5%.
Treats three half-lives like thirds. Halving is repeated multiplication by 1/2, not a straight-line drop.
25% is what is left after two half-lives. Trap: stopping one halving early.
6.25% is what is left after four half-lives. Trap: halving one time too many.

p: A half-life is the time it takes for half of a radioactive sample to decay. After each half-life, half of what is left remains.
So the amount left is (1/2) raised to the number of half-lives. This is repeated halving, not subtracting the same amount each time.

q64.eli: Imagine eating half of a pizza, then half of what is left, then half again. After three bites of this kind, only one eighth of the pizza remains.
mem: Remaining after n half-lives = (1/2)^n

fm.f: Fraction left = (1/2)^n, where n = number of half-lives
fm.why: Each half-life multiplies the remaining amount by 1/2.

q64.trap: Counting one half-life too few (25%) or too many (6.25%). Count the halvings carefully.

ox: Lithium is an alkali metal on the far left. It has a low effective nuclear charge and loses its outer electron easily, so its ionization energy is low.
Sodium is below lithium in the same group. Its outer electron is farther from the nucleus, so it is even easier to remove.
Carbon is in the same period as fluorine but has fewer protons pulling in. Trap: picking a nonmetal without comparing it to fluorine.
Correct. Fluorine is at the top right (excluding noble gases). It has a small radius and a high effective nuclear charge, so its electrons are held tightly.

p: Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an outer electron from an atom. A higher value means the electron is held tighter.
It rises as you go across a period (more protons, same shell) and as you go up a group (outer electrons are closer to the nucleus).

ox: Correct. An outer electron drops into the inner-shell hole and releases the energy as an X-ray.
Alpha emission removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Electron capture does not do that.
Positron emission is another way for the nucleus to turn a proton into a neutron. It is an alternative to capture, not what follows it.
